prompt: Two accounts of the shop's organisation still have nothing but their default VPC in `sa-east-1`. Can those two VPCs be peered so that machines in one reach the other?
hint: Compare the two ranges.

choices.text: Yes, because both accounts belong to the same organisation
choices.why: Belonging to one organisation decides who may ask for a peering, not whether the two ranges can be routed to each other.

choices.text: No: both use `172.31.0.0/16`, so their ranges overlap
choices.why: Right. Every default VPC has the same range, so an address in one is also an address in the other, and no route can tell them apart.

choices.text: Yes, once the second account accepts the request
choices.why: Accepting is a step of every peering, and it does not get past the overlap. AWS refuses a peering between overlapping ranges.

choices.text: Only if the two VPCs sit in different zones
choices.why: A VPC spans every zone of its region; it does not sit in one. The trouble is the range, which zones do not change.

prompt: A fresh moto account answers `[]` to `describe-internet-gateways`. What does the VPC that AWS makes in every new account carry that moto's lacks?
hint: Why is every default subnet open from the first minute?

choices.text: A NAT gateway in each of its zones
choices.why: A NAT gateway is something you build and pay for by the hour; no default VPC comes with one.

choices.text: Nothing more; AWS's default VPC is closed as well
choices.why: AWS's default VPC is open on purpose, so that a first machine can be reached. moto is the one that left the gateway out.

choices.text: A gateway to the internet, and a route to it
choices.why: Right. With the flag that hands out public addresses, that makes every default subnet public. moto creates neither piece.

choices.text: An internet gateway with no route pointing at it
choices.why: A gateway nobody routes to would leave the subnets private. AWS adds the route as well.

prompt: Somebody suggests a `/24` for the shop's production VPC, "to save addresses". Why does the lesson take a `/16` instead?
hint: What does a private address cost, and what does running out cost?

choices.text: A `/24` is smaller than the smallest range AWS accepts for a VPC
choices.why: The smallest is a `/28`, so a `/24` would be accepted. Size is not the objection.

choices.text: Private addresses are free, and a VPC's range cannot be swapped later
choices.why: Right. Nothing is saved by a small range, and a VPC that runs out of room is a migration.

choices.text: AWS bills a VPC by the number of private addresses its range holds, used or not
choices.why: The price list charges public IPv4 addresses in use, not the private range of a VPC.

choices.text: Spreading across three zones takes a `/16` at least
choices.why: Three zones need three subnets, which a `/24` could hold as three small ones. The reason is room, not a rule about zones.

prompt: How many addresses does the range `10.20.0.0/16` hold?
hint: 16 bits are left free.

prompt: `create-vpc` has just returned. Which of these does the new VPC already hold? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last three commands of the transcript counted them.

choices.text: A main route table
choices.why: Right. One table, with a `local` route for the VPC's range.

choices.text: One subnet in each zone
choices.why: That is the default VPC's arrangement. A VPC you create has no subnets until you make them.

choices.text: A security group called `default`
choices.why: Right. Lesson 18 reads its rules.

choices.text: A default network ACL
choices.why: Right. `IsDefault` came back `True`; lesson 18 reads it too.

choices.text: An internet gateway
choices.why: A gateway is created and attached separately, in lesson 17. A new VPC reaches nothing outside itself.

prompt: How many Availability Zones does one subnet live in?
hint: It is the reason the plan has nine subnets rather than three.

choices.text: Every zone of the region, like the VPC that holds it
choices.why: That is true of the VPC and false of the subnet. A subnet is pinned to one zone when it is created.

choices.text: Two, so that it survives losing one
choices.why: Surviving a zone is done with a subnet in each zone, not with one subnet in two.

choices.text: Exactly one, fixed for good when the subnet is created
choices.why: Right. So each tier needs one subnet per zone: three tiers in three zones are nine.

choices.text: Whichever zone its first machine starts in
choices.why: It is the other way round: the subnet's zone decides where its machines run.

prompt: A subnet is created as a `/22`. How many of its addresses can be given to machines?
hint: A `/22` leaves 10 bits free, and AWS keeps the same number in every subnet.

prompt: Whatever its size, every subnet loses ___ addresses to AWS: the network address, the router, the DNS resolver, one for future use and the broadcast address.
hint: Count the list.

prompt: Match each address of the subnet `public-b`, `10.20.16.0/20`, to what AWS uses it for.
hint: The reserved ones are the first four and the last; work out where the `/20` ends.
right_distractors: the first address a machine can be given

prompt: A year on, the shop wants a fourth tier, `cache`, in all three zones, and the nine subnets are busy. Which plan does AWS accept without moving anything?
hint: Two rules from the section: a subnet's range is fixed, and a subnet lives in one zone.

choices.text: Widen the three `app` subnets from `/20` to `/19` and share them
choices.why: A subnet's range cannot be changed after it is created; growing one means replacing it and moving what is inside.

choices.text: Three new `/20`s taken from the spare blocks, one per zone
choices.why: Right. The plan kept seven `/20`s free from `10.20.144.0` up, exactly for a tier nobody had thought of.

choices.text: One `/20` from the spare room, shared by the three zones
choices.why: One subnet lives in one zone, so a single `/20` gives the cache tier one zone and no survival.
Those lie outside `10.20.0.0/16`, and a subnet outside the VPC's ranges is refused as invalid, as the transcript showed.

prompt: moto accepted `10.20.250.0/29` and reported 3 available addresses. What does AWS do with the same request?
hint: The section gives the sizes AWS allows.

choices.text: Accepts it with 3 usable addresses, like moto
choices.why: Here moto is more lenient than AWS. The arithmetic is right; the size is not allowed.

choices.text: Accepts it with all 8 addresses usable, since it is tiny
choices.why: The five reserved addresses do not shrink with the subnet, which is why small subnets are so costly.

choices.text: Refuses it: the smallest subnet AWS accepts is a `/28`
choices.why: Right. A subnet runs from `/28` to `/16`. That refusal was not run in the lab, because moto does not make it.

choices.text: Accepts it once a quota increase is approved
choices.why: A quota counts things, such as ranges per VPC. The size limit of a subnet is not a quota.

prompt: Why does the loop in `16-vpc.sh` end its `aws ec2 create-subnet` line with `< /dev/null`?
hint: Where does `read` get its lines from?

choices.text: So that `aws` cannot eat the plan's lines
choices.why: Right. The loop's input is the pipe from `plan.py`; a command inside that reads it would swallow the lines and end the loop early.

choices.text: To throw away the error messages `aws` prints
choices.why: Errors go to the standard error, and `< /dev/null` touches only the input. A refusal would still be printed.

choices.text: To run the nine `create-subnet` calls at the same time
choices.why: Redirecting input changes nothing about order; the loop still creates one subnet after another.

choices.text: To answer a confirmation question `aws` would ask
choices.why: `create-subnet` asks nothing before acting. The redirection is about what `aws` could read, not about a prompt.

prompt: What makes a subnet public?
hint: Where would a packet for the internet be sent?

choices.text: `MapPublicIpOnLaunch` set to `True` on the subnet
choices.why: That flag hands a starting machine a public address, and an address with no route out goes nowhere.

choices.text: A `0.0.0.0/0` route to an internet gateway
choices.why: Right. Public is a route, not a setting; lesson 17 adds that route for the three public subnets.

choices.text: A `Name` tag that starts with `public`
choices.why: The shop's `public-a` is named that way and is private today. A tag is a word for people.

choices.text: An IPv6 `/64` associated with the subnet, which is public by nature
choices.why: IPv6 addresses are globally unique, but without a route to a gateway they reach nothing either.

prompt: A subnet has `MapPublicIpOnLaunch` set to `True`, and its route table holds only the `local` route. A machine starts there and gets a public address. Can somebody on the internet open a connection to it?
hint: A connection needs packets in both directions.

choices.text: Yes: a public address is reachable by definition
choices.why: The address is a label. Without a route to an internet gateway, nothing carries traffic between it and the internet.

choices.text: Yes, as long as its security group allows the port
choices.why: A security group filters traffic that arrives; it cannot make traffic arrive. The missing piece is the route.

choices.text: No: its route table has no way out of the VPC
choices.why: Right. This is the lesson's idea in one case: a subnet is public because of its route table, and this one is private whatever the flag says.

choices.text: Over IPv6 alone, which needs no gateway
choices.why: IPv6 needs a route to a gateway too, and this table has none for any destination outside the VPC.

prompt: `describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=$pa` answered `[]` for `public-a`. What does that mean?
hint: Every subnet uses some route table.

choices.text: The subnet has no route table, so its packets go nowhere
choices.why: There is no such thing as a subnet without a table: one with no association of its own uses the main one.

choices.text: It uses the main route table, without an association of its own
choices.why: Right. The main table answers for every subnet nobody associated with another one.

choices.text: The filter's name is wrong, so the search matched nothing
choices.why: The filter is a real one; lesson 17 uses it again and it finds the table once there is an explicit association.

choices.text: The subnet is public, since private subnets are the ones with an associated table
choices.why: Both kinds have tables. What decides public or private is what the table says, not whether it is associated by name.

prompt: The shop's VPC, `10.20.0.0/16`, needs a second range. Which of these does AWS accept?
hint: Three of them break a rule the section names.

choices.why: It is half of the VPC's own primary range. moto accepted it; AWS refuses an overlap.
A VPC whose primary range is in `10.0.0.0/8` cannot add one from `192.168.0.0/16`, and it is also the office's range.
It comes from `172.16.0.0/12`, which a VPC with a `10.x` primary cannot add, and it is every default VPC's range besides.
Right. It is the block set aside for carrier networks, it overlaps nothing in the shop's plan, and AWS allows it beside a `10.x` range.

prompt: Every IPv6 address AWS gives a VPC is globally unique. What keeps a machine with one from being reached from outside?
hint: Lesson 17 builds it.

choices.text: A private IPv6 range that AWS hands out instead, like `10.0.0.0/8`
choices.why: There is no such range on AWS: the `/56` comes from AWS's public pool.

choices.text: A NAT gateway that translates the address
choices.why: NAT is how private IPv4 reaches out. IPv6 has no translation to do, since the address is already public.

choices.text: An egress-only internet gateway
choices.why: Right. For IPv6, private is a gateway that only opens outwards.

choices.text: The size of the `/64`, too large to be scanned
choices.why: A large space is hard to guess, but an address that leaks is reached anyway. Hiding is not a filter.

prompt: On AWS, a developer launches a database in a default subnet of `sa-east-1` without choosing anything. What has happened?
hint: Put together the flag and the route of the default VPC on AWS.

choices.text: It has a public address and a route to the internet; its security group is all that stands between it and the world
choices.why: Right. On AWS the default subnet hands out public addresses and routes `0.0.0.0/0` to an internet gateway. That is the unsafe arrangement the default hands you.

choices.text: Nothing risky: a default subnet is private until somebody adds a route
choices.why: That is moto's default VPC. AWS's comes with the gateway and the route already in place.

choices.text: It has a public address but no route, so it cannot be reached
choices.why: The address part is right. The route is there too on AWS: the default VPC's main table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to its gateway.

choices.text: The launch fails, since databases need a VPC created by hand
choices.why: The default VPC accepts anything launched without naming a VPC. That is why it collects the accidents.

prompt: Put the steps of building the shop's VPC in the order the lesson takes them.
hint: A range is chosen before anything is created, and a subnet needs a VPC.
items: choose a range that overlaps no other network of the shop
create the VPC with that range and its tags
work out one `/20` per zone and tier with `plan.py`
create the nine subnets from the plan
give the public tier a route table with a route to an internet gateway
trap: The route table comes last: it is lesson 17, and until then all nine subnets are private.

prompt: Suppose the data tier used a `/24` in each of the three zones instead of a `/20`. How many addresses would the whole tier offer to machines?
hint: One `/24` first, then three of them.

prompt: Which of these did the lab show moto doing differently from AWS? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of the five are things both do the same way.

choices.text: Its default VPC has no internet gateway
choices.why: Right. AWS's has one attached, with a route to it.

choices.text: It refuses a subnet that overlaps another
choices.why: Both refuse it, with `InvalidSubnet.Conflict` in moto's case.

choices.text: It accepts a `/29` subnet
choices.why: Right. AWS's smallest subnet is a `/28`.

choices.text: It keeps five addresses of every subnet
choices.why: Both do: 251 in a `/24` and 4,091 in a `/20`.

choices.text: It accepts a second range that overlaps the first
choices.why: Right. moto took `10.20.128.0/17`; AWS refuses an overlap.
